claims.text: At stage-3 the refund endpoint saves the order as refunding with an order.refund-requested outbox row and answers 202; DonHang.Api makes no call to DonHang.Payments for a refund.

In choreography no part directs the saga: each service reacts to the others' messages and decides its own next step. In orchestration one orchestrator keeps the saga's state, sends each service a command and picks the next step from each reply.
claims.source_hint: glossary saga-choreography, saga-orchestration; Richardson, Microservices Patterns, ch. 4 (saga coordination)

claims.text: Payments binds payments.refund-requests to the topic exchange donhang.orders with exactly order.refund-requested, and declares its own exchange donhang.payments for its answers.
Notifications binds notifications.order-events to donhang.orders with order.*, so it also receives order.refund-requested (and order.refunded, order.refund-failed) and emails the customer about it.
Payments publishes payment.refunded or payment.refund-failed to donhang.payments; DonHang.Api binds orders.payment-events there with payment.*.

PaymentEventsConsumer.HandleAsync picks the step from the routing key: payment.refunded -> CompleteRefundAsync (order cancelled, order.refunded row), payment.refund-failed -> FailRefundAsync (back to paid, order.refund-failed row).

An unknown routing key throws PoisonMessageException, which OnReceivedAsync turns into BasicRejectAsync with requeue: false (RabbitMQ does not deliver it again); the order is not changed and stays refunding.

docs/design/refund-design.md states that no service directs the refund chain (choreography), that following one refund means reading the bindings and consumers of three services, and that there is no orchestrator: three steps, two failure paths, choreography is enough.
An event says something has happened, for whoever listens; a command asks one named receiver to do something.
claims.source_hint: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Event Message vs Command Message

claims.text: An orchestrator is a role, not a deployment: it can live inside a service that already takes part in the saga, provided its state is saved and survives a restart.
claims.source_hint: Richardson, Microservices Patterns, ch. 4 (orchestrator as a saga class inside a participating service)

claims.text: Opinion: choreography fits when a saga has few steps and failure paths (as the refund); when they grow, an orchestrator's single place tends to pay for its extra part, which every step depends on.
claims.source_hint: docs/design/refund-design.md:84-85; Richardson, Microservices Patterns, ch. 4 (benefits and drawbacks of each)
